vignette:
He is a 73-year-old man, a former journalist who spent decades in foreign bureaus, chasing stories that most people only glimpse on the evening news. He lives alone now in a small apartment cluttered with newspapers he cannot bring himself to throw away, though he no longer reads them. He is divorced, and his two children live on the opposite coast. When he speaks of them, his voice softens, but he quickly adds, “They have their own lives. I don’t want to be a burden.”

The trauma happened fifteen years ago, during what was supposed to be a routine assignment covering a humanitarian aid convoy in a conflict zone. He had embedded with a local relief team, driving through a city that had been shelled for weeks. The convoy stopped at a checkpoint. He remembers the heat, the dust, the way the children pressed against the wire fence. Then the explosion—a massive truck bomb detonated by an armed group. He was thrown against a concrete wall, his eardrums ruptured. He watched the aid workers, people he had just been laughing with, die in front of him. He crawled through the rubble, trying to help, but there was nothing left.

He was evacuated, medically treated, and sent home. He tried to write the story—it was his job, his identity—but the words wouldn’t come. Every sentence felt like a betrayal of the dead. He began to avoid newsrooms, then news itself. He would change the channel when a report from that region came on. He stopped answering calls from editors. Eventually, he retired early, telling himself he was just “tired of the grind.”

Now, fifteen years later, the explosion still lives in his body. He hears it in sudden noises—a car backfiring, a door slamming, the clatter of a dropped pan in the kitchen. Each time, his chest tightens, his breath catches, and he finds himself scanning the room for exits. He avoids crowds, especially any gathering near a large vehicle. He once walked out of a grocery store because a delivery truck idled too close to the entrance. He tells his therapist he feels like a coward, but he cannot make himself stay.

Sleep is a battleground. He wakes at 3 a.m., drenched in sweat, the image of the aid workers’ faces pressing against his closed eyelids. He keeps a lamp on all night because the dark feels like the inside of that collapsed building. He drinks two glasses of wine before bed to quiet the racing thoughts, but it only helps for a few hours. The nightmares have become so vivid that he dreads closing his eyes.

His relationships withered. His wife—now ex-wife—tried to understand, but she grew exhausted by his irritability, his sudden anger at small things like a misplaced key, his refusal to talk about what happened. He pushed her away, convinced that anyone who got close would eventually get hurt. The divorce was quiet, almost inevitable.

He tried therapy once before, but the therapist wanted him to “process the event” by writing it down, and he could not. The act of writing—once his lifeblood—now feels like reopening a wound. He types only to pay bills. His old notebooks sit in a box under his bed, taped shut.

At 73, he feels old and hollow. He spends most days in his recliner, watching old black-and-white movies, anything without news. He has no interest in current events. He tells himself that the world has become too dangerous, but he knows it is really himself who has become too fragile. He came to see this current therapist only after his daughter begged him, and because the nightmares became unbearable. He is polite, articulate, and deeply exhausted. He wants relief, but he also fears what it would mean to let go of the pain—as if that would be a betrayal of the people he could not save. He is a man who once chronicled the world’s stories, and now feels that his own story has been over for a long time.
